source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Benchmark of 3,400 step-by-step solutions with human-marked earliest error. Tests whether a scorer finds the one fatal step (gap 1). Most open PRMs fail on hard (Olympiad-level) problems and lose to prompted general models used as critics.
numbers: 3,400 cases; GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH subsets; F1 of error-case and correct-case accuracy. Average F1 from the figure: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5; open PRMs roughly 26-58. The table layout was garbled in text extraction, so only these figure averages are used.
quote: Existing PRMs typically fail to generalize to more challenging math problems beyond GSM8K and MATH.
limits: Math only. Tests a scorer on given solutions, not a search loop. Annotated errors are the earliest error, not fatal-refutation items as in chess.
agent_relevance: A step-scoring evaluator misses the earliest error on hard items. Test our judge on ProcessBench-style items before trusting tree pruning.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Sample, Scrutinize and Scale: Effective Inference-Time Search by Scaling Verification
finding: Plain random sampling plus LLM self-verification (no tree) beats o1-Preview on several benchmarks and keeps scaling after majority voting saturates. Verification improves as more candidates are sampled (implicit scaling). Frontier models verify poorly out of the box.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Pro, correct counts. Pass@1: AIME 1/15, MATH 426/500, LiveBench Math 104/200, LiveBench Reasoning 63/140. Consistency@200: 4/15, 460/500, 118/200, 75/140. Verification@200: 8/15, 467/500, 135/200, 97/140. o1-Preview@1: 7/15, 428/500, 131/200, 95/140. On their verification benchmark o1-preview still fails to identify 20-30% of wrong responses; GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are only marginally above random.
quote: The paper states false positives generally have a more severe impact on downstream performance than false negatives (Table 4 text).
limits: Small AIME n=15. Verifier is the same model family. Gemini 1.5 era.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for gaps 2 and 3: with equal sampling, a verification pass is the lever, and false positives hurt more than false negatives. A generate-then-verify chain is the baseline tree search must beat.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 self-critique loops lower accuracy; a sound external verifier gives large gains, and merely re-prompting with the verifier's pass/fail keeps most of the benefit. Plain sampling with a sound check also beats the critique loop in Game of 24.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Standard prompting / LLM+LLM critique / LLM+sound verifier / sampling k=25: Game of 24 5% / 3% / 36-38% / 42%; Graph Coloring 16% / 2% / 34-38% / 44%; Mystery Blocksworld 4% / 0% / 6-10% / 14%; Blocksworld 40% / 55% / 60-87% / 72%. LLM verifier accuracy: Game of 24 87.0% (3567/4100), Blocksworld 72.4% (362/500), Mystery Blocksworld 71.8% (359/500).
quote: the verifier requires high accuracy or else the overall system will encounter compounding errors
limits: GPT-4 only, 100 items per domain, 2024. Table text partly garbled; Blocksworld is the exception where self-critique rose. Column mapping for the sound-verifier variants taken from the row order.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 answer for planning-style tasks: the check must be sound (code). A shallow exhaustive check helps; LLM self-judgment does not. Sound check plus resampling is simple and strong.

source: Gao, Schulman, Hilton (2022) Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
finding: Optimizing hard against a proxy reward (RL or best-of-n) raises the proxy score while the gold score first rises then falls. Best-of-n follows a different functional form from RL. Coefficients scale smoothly with reward-model size.
numbers: Synthetic gold-RM setup. Best-of-n gold reward fits R(d)=d(alpha - beta*d) in d=sqrt(KL); RL is slower than BoN per unit KL. Exact coefficients not extracted.
quote: Optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart's law.
limits: Preference reward models, not step-level PRMs; synthetic labels; 2022 models.
agent_relevance: Search strength (n, depth) is a Goodhart dial: more search against a fixed evaluator eventually hurts. Cap search per evaluator quality (gap 6).

source: Tiwari et al. (2026) Reward Under Attack: Robustness and Hackability of Process Reward Models
finding: State-of-the-art open PRMs can be pushed to high scores on logically flawed reasoning by short optimized token strings, and RL against a PRM yields reward without accuracy. PRMs are insensitive to style but inconsistent on semantic corruption. A measured blind-spot class (gap 6).
numbers: Skywork-o1-Open-PRM 1.5B/7B and Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B. Optimized 100-token suffix pushes reward above 0.9 on flawed reasoning (training reward 0.11 to 0.95; 8 AIME24 trajectories, transfer to 8 held-out AIME25). GRPO on Skywork: mean PRM reward 0.641 vs base policy 0.246; rephrasing drops it to 0.472; style share 0.169 of 0.395 total gain = 43%. Style changes move reward by less than 0.1.
quote: optimized 100-token adversarial sequences push rewards above 0.9 on logically flawed reasoning
limits: Preprint. Few trajectories (8+8). Math PRMs only; gradient access for the strongest attack.
agent_relevance: Learned evaluators have exploitable blind spots that an optimizer finds. A held-out adversarial test of our own evaluator is justified. Gap 6 partly closed: class shown for PRMs, not for our evaluator.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) One Token to Fool LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Generative reward models and LLM judges accept empty 'master key' answers such as ':' or 'Thought process:' as correct. Master-RMs trained with adversarial negatives fix this attack family.
numbers: False positive rates: punctuation-only up to 35% on GPT-4o; 'Thought process:' 60-90% on LLaMA3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct across benchmarks; General-Verifier 66.8% on MATH with one blank space; Master-RM near 0%. Abstract: FPR as high as 80%.
quote: superficial inputs ... can consistently elicit false positive rewards without any substantive reasoning
limits: Reference-based judging with a gold answer, a different setting from step search. Patch is attack-specific; new attacks after patching not tested.
agent_relevance: LLM-judge false-positive floor is not small. Gap 6: patching one attack family worked here, but whether the class closes is untested.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: With an automatic verifier, coverage grows near log-linearly with number of samples, so cheap resampling plus a real check scales. Without a verifier, majority vote and reward models plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples), above single-sample SOTA 43%. CodeContests Gemma-2B coverage 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples. MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct coverage 82.9% (100 samples) to 98.44% (10,000), but vote or reward-model selection only 40.50% to 41.41%.
quote: common methods for picking from a sample collection (majority voting and reward models) plateau beyond several hundred samples
limits: Coverage is not accuracy unless a verifier exists; compute counted per sample, not per token. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: with a code-checked verifier (false positives about 0) plain sampling is hard to beat; the gap to coverage grows with sample count when the verifier is weak.

source: Guan et al. (2025) rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking
finding: A search-success case (gap 7): MCTS with a learned process preference model (PPM) trained on code-verified Q-values. Code execution filters candidate steps. Ablation: PPM beats a Q-value-only PRM, and both beat best-of-N with an outcome model.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B MATH 58.8 to 90.0; AIME 8/15 (53.3%). Table 8 (7B policy): ORM best-of-N MATH 82.6 / AIME 26.7; PQM (Q-value labels) MCTS 88.2 / 46.7; PPM MCTS 89.4 / 50.0. Inference: 32 candidates per step, 4 rollouts per step; mean generated tokens per problem 5,453 (MATH), 15,693 (AIME 2024), 3,299 (GSM8K).
limits: No equal-token comparison with plain sampling in the paper. Four rounds of training of policy and PPM is a large fixed cost. Math only. Authors' own report.
agent_relevance: Search works when the value is trained from code-checked outcomes; the raw Q-value (code-derived but noisy) is 1.2 MATH points below the learned PPM. Gap 7 partly closed: rStar survives only with trained step values, and it is not shown to beat budget-matched sampling.

source: Ugadiarov et al. (2026) Revisiting Tree Search for LLMs: Gumbel and Sequential Halving (ReSCALE)
finding: AlphaZero-style tree search for LLM reasoning gets worse at the largest budgets because it over-exploits a few actions. Gumbel + Sequential Halving at the root restores monotonic scaling.
numbers: Llama2-7B SFT, GSM8K and Game24, three budget levels. Large budget: AlphaZero 53.6% GSM8K and 82.9% Game24; ReSCALE 58.4% and 85.3%; Best-of-N on GSM8K 53.4%. Ablation (GSM8K, 50 simulations, width 24, depth 16, 3 seeds): full 60.1 +/- 0.9%; without Sequential Halving -4.7; without Gumbel -1.7.
quote: accuracy drops as the search budget increases
limits: One small base model with a learned value net; budgets given as levels. Not a reasoning model.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the root-selection rule decides whether more budget helps or hurts. Standard AlphaZero at Large budget (53.6) is no better than Best-of-N (53.4).

source: Gao et al. (2024) Interpretable Contrastive Monte Carlo Tree Search Reasoning (SC-MCTS*)
finding: Component ablation of MCTS for LLM planning. The UCT constant copied from earlier work (default 1) fails; a tuned C helps. Accuracy rises until about 7 iterations, then gains shrink.
numbers: Blocksworld step 6 hard mode: MCTS base 55.92%; all parts 80.92% (+25.00). Tuned UCT C added 5.27; backprop refinement 1.97; multi-RM 3.29. Base MCTS reward in the ablation was pseudo-random.
quote: the constant C of RAP-MCTS is too small to function effectively
limits: Single dataset (Blocksworld); authors say C needs re-tuning on new datasets. Ablation by the proposing group.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: parameters are task-specific and the default can fail. Avoid parameter-heavy trees or budget a tuning set per task type.

source: Choraria et al. (2026) Know Thy Reasoner: Not All Language Models Explore Alike
finding: Pass@16 test of breadth (iid sampling) vs depth (MCTS-style prefix branching, or self-refine) on DeepMath level 9 at equal token budget, across base, instruct and RLVR checkpoints of Qwen3, OLMo-3 and Nemotron-3. Depth helps post-trained models and hurts base models.
numbers: Pass@16 baseline vs ENT (entropy branching) / SR (self-refine) lift: Qwen3-4B base 0.9004 vs 0.6377 (-29.2%) / 0.6406 (-28.9%); Qwen3-4B instruct +0.65% / +0.54%; Qwen3-4B RLVR 0.6885 to 0.7471 (+9.3%) / +7.9%; OLMo-3 7B base +6.7% / +3.8%; OLMo-3 instruct +20.0% / +19.0%; OLMo-3 RLVR +15.3% / +8.5%; Nemotron-3 30B base -16.6% / -10.3%; Nemotron instruct +29.0% / +39.1%. 1,024 DeepMath problems, N=16 rollouts, 7,168 to 11,264 token limits.
limits: Pass@16 not single-answer accuracy; branching settings tuned on Qwen3-4B only; token limits may truncate RLVR traces (Qwen RLVR baseline 0.69 sits below base 0.90). Not full UCT.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: on 2025-26 post-trained and RLVR models depth is neutral to helpful, not uniformly worse than sampling; on high-diversity base models it is harmful. Choice depends on the model's diversity profile.

source: Liao et al. (2025) Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning
finding: In long-CoT models the first reasoning step strongly shapes the answer and a bad first step is rarely recovered. A measured trap analogue (gap 8). Early pruning of candidate first steps with a reward model saves tokens.
numbers: Accuracy % with forced correct vs incorrect first step: DS-R1-Qwen-1.5B 95.4 vs 64.4; 7B 94.8 vs 28.5; 32B 100.0 vs 85.8; Qwen3-1.7B 96.0 vs 46.6; Qwen3-8B 71.4 vs 37.0; Qwen3-30B-A3B 100.0 vs 74.7; Qwen3-235B-A22B 100.0 vs 78.7. Abstract: up to 40% accuracy drop with a wrong first step.
quote: the model is considerably more likely to arrive at an incorrect final answer (40% accuracy drop)
limits: The wrong step is injected by changing the answer by 1 or 10, not a natural error; math only. Measures recoverability, not natural frequency of traps.
agent_relevance: Spend verification on the first step. Natural trap density is still unmeasured; recovery from a bad step improves with model size.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) FoE: Forest of Errors Makes the First Solution the Best in Large Reasoning Models
finding: In DeepSeek-R1-style models, later alternative solutions inside the chain can mislead an already correct first solution, and reflection does not remove them. Argues extra unverified exploration in one chain can hurt.
numbers: Table 1 (influence of later solutions on the first), Llama-distilled-70b row: 21.2 / 77.9 / 0.9 percent (columns read as misleads / neutral / helps; header not fully recovered). Caption: 93.7% of cases favor the first solution.
limits: I read the introduction and Table 1 only. Column labels inferred. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports caution about second-guessing exploration without a check (gaps 8, 9).

source: Joo & Klabjan (2026) Mitigating Over-Optimization in PRM-Guided Search by Optimizing the Guide
finding: Theory plus experiments: greedy use of PRM scores in search is vulnerable to an extreme-value effect, so non-viable prefixes get spuriously high scores more often as depth grows. A diversity-preserving robust selector beats outcome- and step-level baselines in 14 of 16 settings.
numbers: 14 of 16 settings; per-setting numbers not extracted.
quote: non-viable prefixes become more likely to receive spuriously high scores as reasoning depth increase
limits: Preprint (Aug 2026). I read the abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 6: deeper search against a noisy scorer raises the chance a bad branch ranks first, so tie the depth cap to scorer noise and keep alternatives instead of pruning to the top score.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Controlled puzzles: reasoning models and standard LLMs both collapse to near zero beyond some complexity. At low complexity standard models win at equal inference compute; reasoning effort falls near collapse. Depth evidence on 2025 reasoning models (gap 4, gap 9).
numbers: Three regimes: low (standard LLM better), medium (thinking better), high (both near zero). One model's first error occurs around move 100 in Tower of Hanoi N=10 but by move 4 in River Crossing N=3 (11-move solution); Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) is near perfect.
limits: Disputed: critics blame output token limits and unsolvable River Crossing instances; the paper replies in an appendix. Not MCTS.
agent_relevance: Failure tracks branching and constraint difficulty more than solution length. Cap depth by constraint complexity, and test a reframe before going deeper.

source: Synthesis of d02, d03, d06 (verifier false-positive brackets for gap 2)
finding: No source gives the crossover false-positive rate where tree search beats plain sampling. Only brackets exist from opened papers.
numbers: Sound code check: sampling k=25 reached 42% in Game of 24 vs 36-38% for a verifier loop (d03). LLM verifier accuracy 71.8-87.0%, wrong-answer miss rate 20-30% for o1-preview (d02), judge false positives 35-90% under master keys (d06). rStar-Math (d08) wins with a trained step value.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open as a number. Working rule: with a code check prefer sampling; with an LLM or PRM judge, cap search and add a code check or a held-out judge audit.
